abstract: Abstract Selexipag is an oral selective prostacyclin receptor agonist approved for the treatment of pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) in adults. To date, no treatment targeting the prostacyclin pathway is approved for pediatric patients. Our goal is to identify a pediatric dose regimen that results in comparable exposures to selexipag and its active metabolite JNJ‐68006861 as those shown to be efficacious in adult PAH patients. Extrapolation from the population pharmacokinetic (PK) model developed in adults (GRIPHON study; NCT01106014 ) resulted in the definition of three different pediatric body weight groups (≥9 to <25 kg, ≥25 to <50 kg, and ≥50 kg) with corresponding starting doses (100, 150, and 200 μg twice daily) and maximum allowed doses (800, 1200, and 1600 μg twice daily). The proposed pediatric dose regimen was subsequently tested in a clinical study ( NCT03492177 ), including 63 pediatric PAH patients ≥2 to <18 years of age and a body weight range of 9.9–93.5 kg. The body weight‐adjusted dose regimen for selexipag resulted in comparable systemic exposures to selexipag and its active metabolite in pediatric patients as previously observed in adult PAH patients. Updating the adult selexipag population PK model provided overall consistent parameters and confirmed that the PK characteristics of selexipag and its active metabolite were comparable between pediatric and adult patients. The presented selexipag dose regimen for pediatric PAH patients is considered appropriate for continuing the clinical evaluation of the safety and efficacy of selexipag in pediatric patients ≥2 years of age.

Pediatric study design, participants, and
PK
sampling
NCT03492177
was a prospective, multicenter, open‐label, single‐arm, phase II study to investigate the safety, tolerability, and PK of selexipag and its active metabolite in pediatric PAH patients. The primary objective of the study was to confirm the selexipag starting dose(s) in pediatric PAH patients (≥2 to <18 years of age) that led to similar exposure as in adults at the approved starting dose of 200 μg.
NCT03492177
enrolled pediatric patients with idiopathic PAH, heritable PAH, and PAH associated with congenital heart disease, as well as children with PAH associated with HIV, connective tissue diseases, and drug‐ or toxin‐induced PAH, if they were of WHO Functional Class II or III. Eligible participants were those treated with an endothelin receptor agonist and/or phosphodiesterase‐5 inhibitor, or participants who were not candidates for these therapies. Participants were assigned to three cohorts according to their age (Cohort 1: ≥12 to <18 years; Cohort 2: ≥6 to <12 years; and Cohort 3: ≥2 to <6 years).
Selexipag tablets were available as adult‐size tablets with a dose strength of 200 μg, as well as smaller diameter tablets with a dose strength of 50 μg. Tablets were to be swallowed whole with water when possible. Alternatively, the tablets could also be administered with soft food (i.e., yogurt, apple sauce/puree/mousse, or mashed banana), or the 50‐μg tablets could be dispersed in apple or orange juice.
Starting doses by body weight group are shown in Figure
2
. During a 12‐week titration period, selexipag doses were uptitrated weekly in increments equal to the starting dose until the participant reached their iMTD, or until a maximum dose of 8‐fold of the corresponding starting dose was reached.
FIGURE 2
Pediatric dose extrapolation based on adult population PK model. AUC = combined area under the plasma concentration profile over a 12‐h interval at steady state at the starting dose for selexipag and its active metabolite JNJ‐68006861, weighed by their relative potencies (i.e., AUC
τ,ss,combined
).
Serial blood samples were taken to characterize the selexipag and its active metabolite PK profiles either at steady state of the starting dose (Week 1) for the first five participants of each cohort, or at steady state at the end of the uptitration period (Week 12) for the remaining participants. Blood samples were collected immediately before the selexipag morning dose and at 1, 2, 4, 6, 8, and 12 h postdose. In addition, 3 trough concentrations at steady state were taken from all participants at intermediate doses during the uptitration period. On days of PK sample collection, selexipag was to be administered following a light meal.
The concentrations of selexipag and its active metabolite were measured in plasma using a validated liquid chromatography method with tandem mass spectrometry (LC–MS/MS).
15
Pharmacokinetic parameters of selexipag and its active metabolite were derived for each participant using noncompartmental analysis (NCA) and summarized using descriptive statistics.
Population pharmacokinetics analysis of selexipag and its active metabolite
JNJ
‐68006861 in pediatric
PAH
patients
The estimate of the model parameters from the adult population PK model was used as priors for Bayesian estimation of the PK parameters in pediatric patients. All available pediatric PK data (i.e., PK profiles and trough concentrations) collected from the pediatric study were used to update the adult model. Baseline body weight was used in the model as it was expected that body weight changes over the course of the 12‐week PK sample collection period would be limited and not impacting results. The BAYES estimation algorithm in NONMEM was used to update the parameter estimates of the model, including the parameters related to the covariate effects. In this approach, the point estimate and standard error of a given parameter based on the adult model were used to set up a prior distribution (assumed normal on the natural logarithm of the fixed effect parameters, and inverse‐Wishart for the variance parameters). The pediatric data were then used to obtain posterior distributions for each parameter. No additional covariate search was performed as the knowledge of which covariates impact selexipag and JNJ‐68006861 PK was assumed to be known from the adult data. Standard goodness‐of‐fit plots and simulation‐based approaches (visual predictive checks) were used to qualify the model fitting to the pediatric data available.
16
Then, the individual parameter estimates in pediatric patients with a full PK profile were used to evaluate AUC
τ,ss,combined
at the individual starting dose for each pediatric patient. The AUC
τ,ss,combined
in pediatric patients was compared with the AUC
τ,ss,combined
in adults, as well as the corresponding AUC
τ,ss,combined
obtained by NCA to confirm the dose recommendation in pediatric patients.
The effect of the selexipag administration method (intake with water, with soft food, or as dispersed tablets) was assessed by graphically comparing model‐based AUC
τ,ss,combined
by starting dose group and administration method.
In addition, an alternative approach with a “reduced model” that included only weight as a covariate was first fitted on the adult data and then applied to the pediatric data as described above.
Ethics statement
The study was conducted in accordance with principles for human experimentation as defined in the Declaration of Helsinki principles, International Council for Harmonization and Good Clinical Practice guidelines, and applicable regulations and laws. The study was approved by the institutional review board of each study center and by the competent authority of each country. Informed consent was obtained from each participant before enrollment in the studies, after being advised of the potential risks and benefits of the study, as well as the investigational nature of the study.

Effect of administration method
A graphical assessment by plotting the model‐based AUC
τ,ss,combined
by dose and administration method (Figure
4

Study Highlights
WHAT IS THE CURRENT KNOWLEDGE ON THE TOPIC?
S
elexipag PK is well characterized in the adult population and a treatment regimen where selexipag is gradually titrated to the individual participant's highest tolerated dose has been shown to delay the progression of PAH in adults.
WHAT QUESTION DID THIS STUDY ADDRESS?
Whether the developed pediatric selexipag dosage recommendation based on the population PK model for the adult population results in similar exposures to selexipag and its active metabolite in pediatric PAH patients compared to those observed in adults.
WHAT DOES THIS STUDY ADD TO OUR KNOWLEDGE?
A pediatric, body weight‐adjusted, dose regimen for selexipag in participants ≥2 to <18 years of age resulted in comparable systemic exposures to selexipag and its active metabolite as previously observed in adult PAH patients.
HOW MIGHT THIS CHANGE DRUG DISCOVERY, DEVELOPMENT, AND/OR THERAPEUTICS?
The presented selexipag dose regimen for pediatric patients is considered appropriate for continuing the clinical evaluation of the safety and efficacy of selexipag in pediatric PAH patients ≥2 years of age.
INTRODUCTION
Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) is a life‐threatening disease, characterized by progressive increases in pulmonary artery pressure and pulmonary vascular resistance
1
,
2
and associated with vasoconstriction and proliferation of the vascular smooth muscle cells in the pulmonary arteries, which may result in heart failure and eventual death.
2
,
3
Selexipag (UPTRAVI) is an orally available, selective, and long‐acting nonprostanoid agonist of the prostacyclin (IP) receptor approved for the treatment of PAH (World Health Organization [WHO], Pulmonary Hypertension Group I) in adult patients in more than 70 countries worldwide, including the United States
4
and in the European Union.
5
IP receptor activation by selexipag contributes to vascular smooth muscle relaxation, anti‐proliferation, and anti‐fibrotic effects. Active selexipag is hydrolyzed to its active metabolite JNJ‐68006861 (also known as ACT‐333679), which has a prolonged terminal half‐life compared to that of selexipag. In humans, the exposure to this active metabolite is approximately 3‐ to 4‐fold higher than that of selexipag, and the active metabolite is 37 times more potent than selexipag in activating the IP receptor. The active metabolite is, therefore, considered the major contributor to the pharmacologic effect of selexipag.
1
GRIPHON (
NCT01106014
), the largest clinical phase III study conducted in adult PAH patients to date (
N
= 1156), demonstrated a 40% reduction in the risk of PAH disease progression in adult patients receiving selexipag treatment as compared to placebo.
6
In GRIPHON, and as per the prescribing information for the adult PAH population, selexipag is initiated at a starting dose of 200 μg twice daily and increased weekly in twice daily increments of 200 μg until unmanageable adverse effects associated with prostacyclin use, such as headache, arthralgia, myalgia, nausea, vomiting, or jaw pain, are developed. The dose is then decreased by 200 μg in both daily doses, and this reduced dose is considered the individual maximum tolerated dose (iMTD). The maximum dose allowed for adults is 1600 μg twice daily.
4
,
5
To date, no treatment targeting the prostacyclin pathway is approved for use in pediatric patients. Although the clinical features and course of PAH may differ at times between pediatric and adult patients, the hemodynamic manifestations of increased pulmonary arterial pressure and indexed pulmonary vascular resistance remain the same between these two populations.
7
,
8
Therefore, the rationale to investigate selexipag in pediatric PAH patients is based on the hypothesis that applying an equivalent selexipag dose titration regimen and achieving a similar exposure will result in similar efficacy as established in adult PAH patients.
Selexipag is rapidly absorbed following oral administration and hydrolyzed to its active metabolite by intestinal and hepatic carboxylesterases (CES).
9
,
10
Both selexipag and its active metabolite are mainly excreted via hepatic clearance and metabolized by the cytochrome P450 (CYP) enzyme CYP2C8, and to a lesser extent by CYP3A4.
10
An age‐dependent absolute abundance has been identified for hepatic CES1 and CES2, but the protein abundance seems relatively stable from the age of 1 year and above.
11
In addition, no major differences have been identified in the expression of CYP2C8 and CYP3A4 between the pediatric and adult populations.
12
,
13
,
14
Thus, no age‐related maturation of clearance for selexipag and its active metabolite is expected. In addition, the pharmacokinetics (PK) of selexipag and its active metabolite in pediatric patients ≥2 years of age are expected to differ from adults only with respect to body weight. Based on these assumptions, a body weight‐based dosage recommendation for selexipag targeting the pediatric population was developed and subsequently tested in a clinical study enrolling pediatric PAH patients (
NCT03492177
).
This article presents the population PK modeling approach applied to develop the proposed selexipag dose regimen in the pediatric PAH population, the PK results and population PK analysis of the clinical
NCT03492177
study, and the comparison of pediatric exposure to adults, to confirm the appropriateness of the pediatric doses selected.

Pediatric study design, participants, and
PK
sampling
NCT03492177
was a prospective, multicenter, open‐label, single‐arm, phase II study to investigate the safety, tolerability, and PK of selexipag and its active metabolite in pediatric PAH patients. The primary objective of the study was to confirm the selexipag starting dose(s) in pediatric PAH patients (≥2 to <18 years of age) that led to similar exposure as in adults at the approved starting dose of 200 μg.
NCT03492177
enrolled pediatric patients with idiopathic PAH, heritable PAH, and PAH associated with congenital heart disease, as well as children with PAH associated with HIV, connective tissue diseases, and drug‐ or toxin‐induced PAH, if they were of WHO Functional Class II or III. Eligible participants were those treated with an endothelin receptor agonist and/or phosphodiesterase‐5 inhibitor, or participants who were not candidates for these therapies. Participants were assigned to three cohorts according to their age (Cohort 1: ≥12 to <18 years; Cohort 2: ≥6 to <12 years; and Cohort 3: ≥2 to <6 years).
Selexipag tablets were available as adult‐size tablets with a dose strength of 200 μg, as well as smaller diameter tablets with a dose strength of 50 μg. Tablets were to be swallowed whole with water when possible. Alternatively, the tablets could also be administered with soft food (i.e., yogurt, apple sauce/puree/mousse, or mashed banana), or the 50‐μg tablets could be dispersed in apple or orange juice.
Starting doses by body weight group are shown in Figure
2
. During a 12‐week titration period, selexipag doses were uptitrated weekly in increments equal to the starting dose until the participant reached their iMTD, or until a maximum dose of 8‐fold of the corresponding starting dose was reached.

Serial blood samples were taken to characterize the selexipag and its active metabolite PK profiles either at steady state of the starting dose (Week 1) for the first five participants of each cohort, or at steady state at the end of the uptitration period (Week 12) for the remaining participants. Blood samples were collected immediately before the selexipag morning dose and at 1, 2, 4, 6, 8, and 12 h postdose. In addition, 3 trough concentrations at steady state were taken from all participants at intermediate doses during the uptitration period. On days of PK sample collection, selexipag was to be administered following a light meal.
The concentrations of selexipag and its active metabolite were measured in plasma using a validated liquid chromatography method with tandem mass spectrometry (LC–MS/MS).

Pharmacokinetic parameters of selexipag and its active metabolite were derived for each participant using noncompartmental analysis (NCA) and summarized using descriptive statistics.
Population pharmacokinetics analysis of selexipag and its active metabolite
JNJ
‐68006861 in pediatric
PAH
patients
The estimate of the model parameters from the adult population PK model was used as priors for Bayesian estimation of the PK parameters in pediatric patients. All available pediatric PK data (i.e., PK profiles and trough concentrations) collected from the pediatric study were used to update the adult model. Baseline body weight was used in the model as it was expected that body weight changes over the course of the 12‐week PK sample collection period would be limited and not impacting results. The BAYES estimation algorithm in NONMEM was used to update the parameter estimates of the model, including the parameters related to the covariate effects. In this approach, the point estimate and standard error of a given parameter based on the adult model were used to set up a prior distribution (assumed normal on the natural logarithm of the fixed effect parameters, and inverse‐Wishart for the variance parameters). The pediatric data were then used to obtain posterior distributions for each parameter. No additional covariate search was performed as the knowledge of which covariates impact selexipag and JNJ‐68006861 PK was assumed to be known from the adult data. Standard goodness‐of‐fit plots and simulation‐based approaches (visual predictive checks) were used to qualify the model fitting to the pediatric data available.
16
Then, the individual parameter estimates in pediatric patients with a full PK profile were used to evaluate AUC
τ,ss,combined
at the individual starting dose for each pediatric patient. The AUC
τ,ss,combined
in pediatric patients was compared with the AUC
τ,ss,combined
in adults, as well as the corresponding AUC
τ,ss,combined
obtained by NCA to confirm the dose recommendation in pediatric patients.
The effect of the selexipag administration method (intake with water, with soft food, or as dispersed tablets) was assessed by graphically comparing model‐based AUC
τ,ss,combined
by starting dose group and administration method.
In addition, an alternative approach with a “reduced model” that included only weight as a covariate was first fitted on the adult data and then applied to the pediatric data as described above.
Ethics statement
The study was conducted in accordance with principles for human experimentation as defined in the Declaration of Helsinki principles, International Council for Harmonization and Good Clinical Practice guidelines, and applicable regulations and laws. The study was approved by the institutional review board of each study center and by the competent authority of each country. Informed consent was obtained from each participant before enrollment in the studies, after being advised of the potential risks and benefits of the study, as well as the investigational nature of the study.

Selexipag pediatric dose selection based on adult data
The continuous body weight‐exposure relationship with body weights ranging from 40 to 148 kg, identified in the adult population PK model, was extrapolated to define pediatric body weight categories and starting doses such that, on average, the expected AUC
τ,ss,combined
in a pediatric patient would be comparable to that of a 70 kg adult while not exceeding the exposure in a 50 kg adult receiving a dose of 200 μg. As a result, three different body weight groups (≥9 to <25 kg, ≥25 to <50 kg, and ≥ 50 kg) were defined with corresponding starting doses of 100, 150, and 200 μg twice daily and maximum allowed doses of 800, 1200, and 1600 μg twice daily, respectively (Figure

DISCUSSION
The PK of selexipag has been extensively characterized based on numerous studies conducted in the adult population, including both adult healthy participants and adult PAH patients.
15
,
18
,
19
,
20
,
21
Here, we describe how the adult population PK model
1
has been used to identify the pediatric selexipag dose regimen and we characterize, for the first time, the PK properties of selexipag and its active metabolite in pediatric PAH patients ≥2 years of age. The population PK model developed in adults with PAH, which accounted for the impact of several covariates including body weight, was used to determine the most appropriate selexipag doses and associated body weight categories to ensure similar exposure in pediatrics as seen in adults, while limiting the risk of over‐exposure in the lighter participants of each weight category.
Subsequently, the proposed body weight‐adjusted dose regimen of selexipag was extensively evaluated, based on PK data collected from a total of 62 study participants in the age range of 2–17 years and a body weight range of 9.9–93.5 kg (
NCT03492177
). The results of this study confirmed that across all the tested pediatric body weight groups (≥9 to <25 kg, ≥25 to <50 kg, and ≥ 50 kg) and age cohorts (Cohort 1: ≥12 to <18 years; Cohort 2: ≥6 to <12 years; and Cohort 3: ≥2 to <6 years), the body weight‐based dose regimen resulted in similar exposure (AUC
τ,ss
and maximum concentration at steady state [
C
max,ss
]) as that seen in adult participants from the adult GRIPHON study. Updating the selexipag population PK model provided overall consistent parameters and confirmed that the PK characteristics of selexipag and its active metabolite are similar between pediatric and adult PAH patients. The observed pediatric exposures are also comparable to those previously reported from a study with rich PK sampling following oral selexipag administration in adult PAH patients.
22
In this adult study, when dose normalizing the observed data to the adult starting dose of 200 μg, the geometric mean (95% CI) of the AUC
τ,ss
and maximum concentration [
C
max
] of selexipag were 8.7 (6.5–11.7) ng h/mL and 3.9 (3.0–5.1) ng/mL, respectively and AUC
τ,ss
and
C
max

which is very similar to the exposures observed in the pediatric population (Table
2

). As such, no major differences have been identified with respect to the PK properties of selexipag and its active metabolite between the pediatric and adult populations. The hypothesis that the PK of selexipag and its active metabolite in pediatric patients ≥2 years of age are similar to adults and that differences in exposures between pediatric and adult patients can be explained by differences in body weight only is therefore confirmed.
In clinical practice, the specific requirements for adequate dosage of pediatric patients depend not only on an age‐appropriate efficacious and safe dose regimen but also on the ability of the children to take the medication. For the adult population, selexipag is available as oral tablets, which are to be swallowed whole with water.
3
,
7
For the pediatric study, selexipag was available as both adult‐size tablets and smaller diameter 50‐μg tablets developed specifically to facilitate the administration in pediatric participants.
23
In addition, participants were given the opportunity to take the tablets with soft food or following dispersion in apple or orange juice if needed. Comparing the observed individual exposures between participants swallowing the tablets whole with water, taking the tablets with soft food, or following dispersion in juice did not suggest any relevant difference in PK following any of the administration methods (Figure
4
). Although the actual number of participants taking the tablets with soft food or following dispersion is limited, the available data support that either option can be applied as needed, without any relevant impact on the observed exposures to selexipag and its active metabolite.
The tested body weight‐adjusted dose recommendation for selexipag results in a comparable combined exposure to selexipag and its active metabolite in the pediatric population to the exposure shown to be efficacious in adults. The proposed dose recommendation is, therefore, considered appropriate for further clinical testing of selexipag in the pediatric population. The efficacy and a favorable risk–benefit profile of selexipag for the treatment of PAH in pediatric patients is, however, still to be confirmed. The pediatric dose regimen, as described here, is applied in a double‐blind, placebo‐controlled phase III study (SALTO,
NCT04175600
) evaluating the efficacy, safety, and tolerability of selexipag on top of standard of care in the pediatric population with PAH.
